questions.subject: BIOLOGY
questions.topic: Biotechnology: A Restriction Enzyme and Its Recognition Site
questions.learningObjective: state what a recognition sequence determines about a restriction enzyme's cut
questions.stem: A restriction enzyme cuts double-stranded DNA only where a short sequence occurs in a fixed arrangement. What does the recognition sequence decide?

options.text: Where the cut is placed, since each enzyme binds its own short sequence and cuts within it
How much of the inserted gene the vector can hold, since the sequence sets its final length
options.misconception: believes a recognition site limits how much DNA a vector carries

options.text: Whether the two cut ends will join again, since the sequence decides if the ends are compatible
options.misconception: believes the recognition sequence determines whether two ends can be joined

options.text: How quickly the cut product is made, since the sequence tells the enzyme how many copies to cleave
options.misconception: believes a recognition sequence sets the reaction rate rather than the site

questions.explanation: A restriction enzyme is a protein that recognises a particular short double-stranded sequence and cuts the backbone at a fixed position within or beside it, so the sequence is the address the enzyme reads and the position is where it acts. That precision is what makes the enzyme useful: the same enzyme applied to two different molecules cuts both at the matching sites and nowhere else, which is the basis of every mapping and cloning step that follows. The tempting belief that the sequence sets how much DNA a vector can hold fails because a recognition site is a few bases long and has nothing to do with insert capacity. The belief that the sequence decides whether two ends will join fails because that is a property of the ends produced, which two different enzymes can arrange to be the same. The belief that the sequence sets the reaction rate fails because rate depends on enzyme amount, temperature and substrate, all of which vary while the sequence stays the same.
questions.hint: Ask what the enzyme is reading on the DNA, and what happens at the position it reads.

questions.subject: BIOLOGY
questions.topic: Biotechnology: What a Plasmid Needs to Be a Vector
questions.learningObjective: identify the three features a cloning vector must carry
questions.stem: A small circular piece of bacterial DNA is used to carry a fragment of human DNA into a recipient cell. What must the plasmid have in order to work as a vector?

options.text: An origin of replication, a selectable marker, and a place it can be opened without breaking the rest
A centromere, two telomeres, and matching telomerase enzymes, because these are required of a vector
options.misconception: believes a vector must carry the machinery a linear chromosome needs

options.text: A protein promoter, an anticodon sequence, and a pair of stop codons to halt the reading machine
options.misconception: assembles vector features out of parts of gene expression rather than delivery

options.text: A cell membrane, a cell wall, and a set of ribosomes, so the inserted gene is made at once
options.misconception: believes the vector itself must carry the translation machinery with it

questions.explanation: A vector has three jobs, and the features it needs follow directly from them. It has to be copied inside the recipient, which requires an origin of replication that the host's own machinery can read. It has to be possible to find the cells that received it among the many that did not, which requires a selectable marker. And it has to accept an insert, which requires that it can be opened at a chosen place without destroying the two features it depends on, so the sites are placed away from the origin and the marker. The origin is the feature most often forgotten, and without it the plasmid is carried into the cell but never replicated, so it is eventually lost. The tempting belief that centromeres and telomeres are required fails because those solve the problem of copying and segregating a linear chromosome, and a plasmid is circular and segregates by a different route. The belief that the vector should carry expression parts fails because those matter for making the product, not for delivering the DNA. The belief that it should carry a wall and ribosomes fails because the recipient cell already has both.
questions.hint: Ask what the plasmid must achieve in the recipient cell, and how a failed delivery would be noticed.

questions.subject: BIOLOGY
questions.topic: Biotechnology: What a Selectable Marker Is For
questions.learningObjective: explain how a selectable marker separates transformed from untransformed cells
questions.stem: After a cloning experiment, only a tiny fraction of recipient cells have taken up the plasmid at all. Why does the vector carry a selectable marker?

options.text: It lets only cells that took up the vector survive on a medium that blocks every other cell
It shows whether the insert lies in the right orientation and in the correct reading frame
options.misconception: believes the marker reports the arrangement of the inserted fragment

options.text: It cuts the insert at both ends so that the fragment can be joined into the opened vector
options.misconception: believes the marker performs the cutting that opens the vector

options.text: It copies the inserted fragment many times so that enough material is available for sequencing
options.misconception: believes the marker amplifies the insert rather than selecting for the vector

questions.explanation: A selectable marker answers the question of which cells received the vector, and the usual form of that answer is an enzyme that inactivates an antibiotic so that the medium can carry the antibiotic and only transformed cells grow on it. The word transformed here means carrying the plasmid, not having been genetically altered in any other sense, and because only a small fraction of cells take up a plasmid the selection is what makes the experiment possible at all: without it the culture is a mixture in which the rare cells of interest are buried. The marker selects for the presence of the vector, and that is a real limitation worth stating, because a cell carrying a plasmid that has re-closed without the insert will also survive. The tempting belief that the marker checks the insert fails because that requires a separate test such as a size check or a sequencing read. The belief that it opens the vector fails because opening is done by a restriction enzyme. The belief that it amplifies the insert fails because amplification is done by a polymerase and a pair of primers.
questions.hint: Ask what happens to the cells that did not take up the plasmid when a selection is applied.

questions.subject: BIOLOGY
questions.topic: Biotechnology: What a Reporter Gene Reports
questions.learningObjective: explain how a reporter converts regulatory activity into a detectable signal
questions.stem: A construct places a regulatory region under study next to a gene whose product is easy to detect. What does the reporter gene make possible?

options.text: Whether and when the regulatory region is active, because the signal appears only where it drives expression
How many copies of the regulatory region the construct carries, because the reporter is counted as it builds
options.misconception: believes the reporter's signal reports the number of copies of the region

options.text: Whether the regulatory region has been cut, because cutting the construct in the right place releases it
options.misconception: believes the reporter works by being freed when a restriction enzyme cuts

options.text: Whether a protein binds the regulatory region, because the reporter is itself a DNA-binding protein
options.misconception: believes the reporter binds DNA and so reports occupancy by a factor

questions.explanation: The reporter gene is placed under the control of the region being studied, so whatever makes the region switch on also makes the reporter gene, and the reporter's easy-to-measure product therefore stands in for the activity of the region itself. That substitution is what allows a signal to be read out from something that would otherwise be invisible, and it works for a promoter, an enhancer or any other regulatory region. The important property is that the reporter is downstream of the control in question and nothing else drives it, so signal and activity stay in step. The tempting belief that the signal reports copy number fails because a reporter reading is a measure of transcription, and copy number is measured by a different technique entirely. The belief that cutting releases the reporter confuses a reporter construct with a gene-disruption construct, in which losing a functional gene is the signal. The belief that the reporter binds DNA fails because the reporter is the product whose activity is measured, not the thing doing the measuring.
questions.hint: Ask which switch controls the reporter gene, and what follows if that switch changes.

questions.subject: BIOLOGY
questions.topic: Biotechnology: What a Restriction Map Is For
questions.learningObjective: state what a restriction map predicts and what it cannot reveal
questions.stem: A restriction map records where several enzymes cut one piece of DNA and draws them to scale along its length. What does such a map let a researcher do?

options.text: Predict the fragment sizes any chosen enzyme will give, because the sites are known positions on a measured length
Read the base sequence between any two sites, because the map records every nucleotide position
options.misconception: believes a map of cut sites is also a record of the sequence itself

options.text: Tell whether a gene is switched on in a given cell, because the map shows where regulators bind
options.misconception: believes a physical map of positions reports gene activity in a cell

options.text: Count how many organisms in a sample carry the map, because the map is built from a survey
options.misconception: believes mapping a molecule involves surveying a population of organisms

questions.explanation: A restriction map converts a set of cut sites into a ruler. Once the molecule's total length and the positions of the sites are known, the sizes of the fragments that any chosen enzyme, or any combination of enzymes, will produce follow by subtraction, which means a digest can be designed and its expected bands written down before any gel is run. That is its whole value, and it is a large one when a molecule is too long to sequence directly. The tempting belief that it gives the sequence fails because the map locates positions, not bases, and reading the bases between two sites requires sequencing. The belief that it reports gene activity fails because activity is a property of a cell at a moment, and a map of a purified molecule says nothing about any cell. The belief that it counts organisms fails because the map describes one molecule and is built by cutting, separating and measuring fragments.
questions.hint: Ask what you can calculate from a known total length and a set of marked positions.

questions.subject: BIOLOGY
questions.topic: Biotechnology: Reading a Fragment's Size From Migration
questions.learningObjective: state what band position on a gel reports and what it does not
questions.stem: DNA fragments are run through a gel alongside a ladder of known lengths. What does how far a band has travelled let you determine?

options.text: The fragment's length, since shorter fragments move further through the matrix in the same time
The fragment's base sequence, since the two strands separate and migrate at different speeds
options.misconception: believes a gel reads out the order of bases in a fragment

options.text: How many copies of the fragment are present, since band brightness reports amount directly
options.misconception: believes band intensity reports copy number without any calibration

options.text: The fragment's shape, since circular DNA travels differently however large it happens to be
options.misconception: believes the separation is by shape rather than by size

questions.explanation: The gel separates by size because the matrix is a sieve: small fragments meet less resistance and reach the far end first, so distance travelled is a proxy for length, and the ladder supplies the calibration that turns that distance into a number. Everything about the reading follows from that, including the fact that a small fragment migrates further and that the result is a length in base pairs rather than a mass. The same principle is why a ladder of known sizes is run in the same gel, since the migration depends on the conditions of the run and only fragments in the same run are comparable. The tempting belief that the sequence can be read fails because separation depends on length and not on base order. The belief that brightness reports copy number fails because intensity is not linear in amount without calibration and is affected by how much DNA was loaded. The belief that shape is the variable fails because the effect of conformation is real but secondary, and it is the reason an uncut circular plasmid runs faster than the same plasmid cut once.
questions.hint: Ask what a gel does to fragments of different sizes as they meet the same matrix.

questions.subject: BIOLOGY
questions.topic: Biotechnology: What a Southern Blot Detects
questions.learningObjective: state what a probe hybridisation in a blot reports about a sample
questions.stem: DNA is cut with an enzyme, separated in a gel, transferred to a membrane and then exposed to a labelled single-stranded probe. What does this detect?

options.text: Whether the chosen sequence is in the sample, at the size of the fragment that carries it
The order of the bases in the chosen sequence, because the probe reads them as it binds
options.misconception: believes a labelled probe sequences the region it hybridises to

options.text: Which cells in the sample are making the chosen protein, because the probe is then translated
options.misconception: believes a DNA blot reports protein synthesis in individual cells

options.text: How many copies of the chosen sequence the sample holds, because the probe binds once per copy
options.misconception: believes a single band reports a precise copy number without any control

questions.explanation: The blot is a question with two parts. The gel has already separated the fragments by size, and the transfer to a membrane preserves that separation, so a labelled probe that finds its sequence lights up the band belonging to the fragment that carries it. The result is therefore presence combined with size, which is what makes the technique able to tell one gene from another and to detect a change in fragment length that a plain presence test could not see. The sequence information has been discarded at the gel step and cannot be recovered from the blot. The tempting belief that the probe reads the sequence fails because a probe hybridises by base pairing and reports matching, not ordering. The belief that it reports protein production fails because that requires a different technique working on extracted protein or on messenger RNA. The belief that one band gives a copy number fails because band strength without a known standard does not distinguish one copy from several, and a single band cannot even distinguish one sequence present on two fragments from one present on one.
questions.hint: Ask what the gel step did to the sequence information before the probe was applied.

questions.subject: BIOLOGY
questions.topic: Biotechnology: Why Amplification Needs Two Primers
questions.learningObjective: state what primers contribute that a polymerase reaction cannot start without
questions.stem: A polymerase chain reaction copies one chosen stretch of DNA and cannot begin without a starting point. What do its two primers supply?

options.text: The free ends the polymerase extends from, which fix where copying starts and which strand to read
The two strands of the template, which they separate so the enzyme can read both at once
options.misconception: believes the primers separate the strands rather than the heating step

options.text: The nucleotides to be incorporated, because the reaction holds no free nucleotides of its own
options.misconception: believes the primers supply the building blocks rather than the starting ends

options.text: The heat that separates the strands, because the primers melt the duplex at every repeated step
options.misconception: believes the primers supply the energy that opens the duplex each cycle

questions.explanation: A DNA polymerase can only add nucleotides to an existing three-prime end, so a reaction that begins with template and enzyme alone cannot start, and the primers provide the two free ends that satisfy that requirement. Because one primer pairs with the template on one side and the other pairs on the opposite side, together they also define the two boundaries of the region copied, so the choice of primers is what decides which part of the genome is amplified. The two products made from those primers then serve as templates in the next cycle, which is what turns a single pair of molecules into a doubling population. The tempting belief that the primers separate the strands fails because each cycle is opened by heating, not by the primers. The belief that they supply nucleotides fails because the four free nucleotides are in the reaction at high concentration. The belief that they supply heat fails because heat is supplied by the heating block, and the reaction is repeatedly cooled and rewound to get to that cycle in the first place.
questions.hint: Ask what a polymerase chemically requires at the end of a growing chain, and where the region copied begins.

questions.subject: BIOLOGY
questions.topic: Biotechnology: Cycles Needed to Reach a Million Copies
questions.learningObjective: solve a doubling series for the cycle count that reaches a stated copy number

stimulus.body: Laboratory note (written for this course): An amplification reaction is set up with 10 copies of the target sequence. Every completed cycle doubles the number of copies exactly, with no loss, no inhibition and no saturation, and the copies produced in one cycle are available to be copied in the next. The aim is to obtain at least 1,000,000 copies.

questions.stem: Using only the laboratory note, how many complete cycles are needed, and what is the count after them?

options.text: Seventeen cycles, giving 1,310,720 copies, because sixteen cycles reaches only 655,360
Sixteen cycles, giving 1,310,720 copies, because seventeen would overshoot the million needed
options.misconception: reads the count for the higher cycle count and attaches it to the lower one

options.text: Twenty cycles, giving 1,048,576 copies, because every cycle is taken to double the total twice
options.misconception: counts each cycle as two doublings rather than one

options.text: Ten cycles, giving 10,240 copies, because the note states that a single cycle doubles the copies
options.misconception: uses one doubling per ten cycles and reaches far short of the target

questions.explanation: Sixteen cycles give 10 times 65,536, which is 655,360 and so falls short of a million, while seventeen cycles give 10 times 131,072, which is 1,310,720 and clears it, so seventeen is the smallest number of cycles that works. The answer has to be the smallest sufficient count, because running extra cycles costs time and, in a real reaction, promotes the artefacts that appear when the products start to anneal to one another instead of to their primers. Working backwards is quicker than working forwards: a million divided by ten is 100,000, and the smallest power of two at or above 100,000 is 131,072, which is two to the seventeenth. The tempting belief that sixteen suffices fails because the count for sixteen is below the target. The belief that every cycle counts twice fails because a cycle is one round of separation and copying. The belief that ten cycles is enough fails because ten doublings from ten copies gives 10,240, three orders of magnitude short.
questions.hint: Halve the target repeatedly from a million until you reach ten, and count the halvings.

questions.subject: BIOLOGY
questions.topic: Biotechnology: Subtracting Cut Positions for Fragment Sizes
questions.learningObjective: compute the fragment sizes a double digest of linear DNA produces

stimulus.body: Laboratory note (written for this course): A linear piece of DNA is 10,000 base pairs long. One restriction enzyme cuts it at 1,500 base pairs measured from the left end, and a second enzyme cuts it at 6,000 base pairs measured from the left end. Both cuts are complete, so the digest contains no uncut molecule and no partially cut molecule.

questions.stem: Using only the laboratory note, what fragment sizes should the digest produce?

options.text: 1,500, 4,500 and 4,000 base pairs, from the left end and from the gap between the two cuts
1,500, 6,000 and 2,500 base pairs, taking the two cut positions and their difference
options.misconception: uses the second cut position as though it were a fragment length

options.text: 6,000, 1,500 and 2,500 base pairs, working right to left from the second cut position
options.misconception: starts from the second cut and forgets where the molecule begins

options.text: 10,000, 6,000 and 1,500 base pairs, counting each cut separately without removing what was cut
options.misconception: reports the whole molecule and both cut positions as though they were fragments

questions.explanation: A complete digest of a linear molecule is read by walking along it, and the fragments are the distances from the left end to the first cut, between the two cuts, and from the second cut to the right end. Those distances are 1,500, 6,000 minus 1,500 which is 4,500, and 10,000 minus 6,000 which is 4,000, and they add to 10,000 exactly, which is the check that the answer is right. The same subtraction gives two more figures worth stating: two cuts on a linear molecule always make three fragments, whereas two cuts on a circle make only two, because there is no end to make a terminal fragment. The tempting belief that a cut position is a length fails because a position is measured from an end and a length is not. The belief that the count is three fragments of 6,000, 1,500 and 2,500 fails because those sum to 10,000 but no two of them are adjacent in the molecule. The belief that the whole molecule survives as a fragment fails because complete cutting removes it.
questions.hint: Measure the distance from each end to the nearest cut, and the gap between the two cuts.

questions.subject: BIOLOGY
questions.topic: Biotechnology: Counting Bands From a Circular and a Cut Plasmid
questions.learningObjective: predict band counts and migration order from a circular digest

stimulus.body: Laboratory note (written for this course): A circular plasmid 5,400 base pairs long is digested in two separate lanes of one gel. In lane one a single enzyme with exactly one site on the plasmid was used. In lane two two enzymes were used together whose sites lie 900 base pairs apart on the circle. A ladder of known fragment lengths was run in a third lane of the same gel under the same conditions.

questions.stem: Using only the laboratory note, how many bands does each lane hold, and which moves furthest?

options.text: One band in lane one and two in lane two, with the 900 base pair band furthest down the gel
Two bands in lane one and three in lane two, with the 5,400 band furthest down the gel
options.misconception: counts a linear molecule's fragments while looking at a circular one

options.text: One band in lane one and two in lane two, with the 4,500 base pair band furthest down the gel
options.misconception: believes the larger of the two circular fragments is the one that travels fastest

options.text: One band in lane one and one in lane two, since both enzymes cut the circle at a single place
options.misconception: assumes the two enzymes cut at the same point on the circle

questions.explanation: One cut in a circle opens it into a single linear piece of 5,400 base pairs, so lane one holds one band, and a circular molecule with no cuts would have stayed fast-moving and compact rather than appearing as one band at its true length. Two cuts in a circle make two pieces, not three, because a circle has no ends: the two fragments are 900 base pairs and 5,400 minus 900 which is 4,500, and they add to 5,400. Of those two, the 900 base pair fragment is the smaller and therefore travels furthest through the gel, which is the same size rule that governs any separation. The tempting belief that a circle gives three fragments fails because that count belongs to a linear molecule. The belief that the larger fragment travels furthest fails because migration runs opposite to size. The belief that two enzymes cut at the same point fails because the note places the two sites 900 base pairs apart, so the digest is not a repeat of lane one.
questions.hint: Ask how many pieces a circle becomes with one cut and with two, then use the size rule for migration.

questions.subject: BIOLOGY
questions.topic: Biotechnology: Reading a Three-Cycle Threshold Difference
questions.learningObjective: convert a difference in threshold cycle into a starting-template ratio

stimulus.body: Laboratory note (written for this course): A quantitative amplification reaction is run on two samples under conditions in which the amplification doubles perfectly in every cycle. Sample A reaches the set detection threshold at cycle 22 and sample B at cycle 25. The threshold was set at the same fluorescence level in both wells, no inhibitors are present, and the two wells were loaded with the same reaction volume.

questions.stem: Using only the laboratory note, what does the difference between the two readings say about the starting material?

options.text: Sample A began with eight times the target of sample B, because three cycles is three doublings
Sample B began with eight times the target of sample A, because a later reading is a larger start
options.misconception: reverses the direction, reading a later threshold as a larger amount

options.text: The two began with the same target, because the threshold level was set identically in both wells
options.misconception: believes a shared threshold setting cancels any difference in starting amount

options.text: Sample A began with twice the target of sample B, because a cycle adds only one extra copy
options.misconception: counts a cycle as a single unit rather than as a doubling

questions.explanation: A sample that starts with more target reaches a given threshold in fewer cycles, so sample A, which crosses at 22 rather than 25, started with more. The size of the difference follows from the doubling: three cycles is three doublings, and 2 to the third is 8, so sample A began with eight times the target and sample B with an eighth as much. The direction is the part that trips people up, because the cycle number itself is a measure of how little you started with, so the smaller number is the larger amount. The threshold has to be at one fixed level in both wells for the comparison to mean anything at all, which is exactly what the note stipulates. The tempting belief that a later reading means more target fails because it inverts the whole relationship. The belief that the shared threshold cancels the difference fails because that shared level is what makes the cycle numbers comparable. The belief that a cycle adds one copy fails because a cycle is one doubling, not one increment.
questions.hint: Work out how many times the target doubles in a three-cycle gap, and check which sample crossed first.

questions.subject: BIOLOGY
questions.topic: Biotechnology: Predicting Bands From a Three-Enzyme Map
questions.learningObjective: predict a multi-enzyme digest and recognise comigrating equal fragments

stimulus.body: Laboratory note (written for this course): A restriction map of a linear piece of DNA 12,000 base pairs long shows sites for enzyme Q at 3,000 base pairs, enzyme R at 7,500 base pairs and enzyme S at 10,500 base pairs, each measured from the left end. A complete double-stranded digest using all three enzymes together is run, and the products are separated on a gel under standard conditions with a ladder alongside.

questions.stem: Using only the laboratory note, what does the gel show, and how do the equal fragments behave?

options.text: Fragments of 3,000, 4,500, 3,000 and 1,500, so the two 3,000 fragments appear as one thicker band
Fragments of 3,000, 7,500, 10,500 and 1,500, with each cut site reporting its own band
options.misconception: reports the three cut positions and the terminal fragment as though all were products

options.text: Fragments of 3,000, 4,500 and 4,500, since only the two largest fragments are long enough to see
options.misconception: believes short fragments are lost and mis-reads the two gaps as equal

options.text: Fragments of 4,000 each, since three evenly spaced sites divide the molecule into equal parts
options.misconception: assumes evenly spaced sites cut a molecule into equal-length pieces

questions.explanation: Three sites on a linear molecule make four fragments, and their lengths are 3,000 from the left end to the first site, 7,500 minus 3,000 which is 4,500 between the first and second sites, 10,500 minus 7,500 which is 3,000 between the second and third, and 12,000 minus 10,500 which is 1,500 at the right end. Those four add to 12,000, which is the check on the arithmetic. Because two of them are 3,000 base pairs long they travel together and the gel shows three bands rather than four, with the band at that position looking darker or broader because it holds twice as much DNA. That is a feature of the technique rather than an error, and it is a warning about reading band counts as fragment counts. The tempting belief that each site yields a band fails because sites mark boundaries and not products. The belief that the two gaps are equal fails because 4,500 and 3,000 come from different differences. The belief that even spacing implies even fragments fails because the sites here are not evenly spaced and even if they were, equal spacing would give equal gaps and not equal total pieces.
questions.hint: Subtract consecutive positions, and count how many separate bands the sizes would actually produce.

questions.subject: BIOLOGY
questions.topic: Biotechnology: Reading Identity and a Conserved Block
questions.learningObjective: compute identity over an alignment and interpret a conserved region

stimulus.body: Laboratory note (written for this course): Two protein sequences of 200 residues each are aligned residue by residue. Of the 200 aligned positions, 180 carry the same amino acid in both sequences and 20 carry a different one. In a third and a fourth sequence, a stretch of 24 consecutive residues around position 100 is identical in all four sequences, while the residues on either side of that stretch are about 40 per cent identical from one sequence to another.

questions.stem: Using only the laboratory note, what do the two sets of numbers support?

options.text: The pair is about 90 per cent identical overall, and the four-way block is a site kept under constraint
The pair is about 20 per cent different overall, and the block is a region under no constraint at all
options.misconception: inverts the identity figure and treats perfect identity as freedom to vary

options.text: The pair is about 90 per cent identical overall, and the block is where the pair is least alike
options.misconception: reads the most conserved stretch as though it were the most divergent one

options.text: The pair is about 40 per cent identical overall, and the block is an artefact of the alignment
options.misconception: quotes the side-of-block figure as the overall identity for the pair

questions.explanation: Identity is matched positions divided by aligned positions, so 180 out of 200 is 90 per cent, and 20 differences out of 200 is 10 per cent rather than 20 per cent, which is the first trap. The block behaves differently from its surroundings in a way that carries information: it is identical in all four sequences while the regions flanking it vary at about 40 per cent from one sequence to another. A stretch that is conserved across separate sequences while its neighbours are not is the standard signature of a site whose exact form is required, because a change there would remove the function and so has been removed by selection. That inference is a strong hint rather than a proof, and the usual qualification is that the block may be the part of the protein that is hardest to align, so its conservation can be an artefact of the method. The tempting belief that 20 differences is 20 per cent fails because the denominator is 200 and not 20. The belief that the block is the least alike fails because it is identical in all four. The belief that 40 per cent is the pair's identity fails because that figure describes the flanks across four sequences, not the pair overall.
questions.hint: Divide the number of matching positions by the number of aligned positions, then compare the block with its surroundings.

questions.subject: BIOLOGY
questions.topic: Biotechnology: Separating a Single Insert, a Double Insert and an Empty Vector
questions.learningObjective: design a screen that distinguishes the possible products of a ligation
questions.stem: A plasmid has been opened, a fragment has been joined in, and colonies have grown on a selective plate. Describe a test that would tell apart cells carrying one insert, cells carrying two inserts and cells carrying only re-closed vector.

answer.exemplar: Screen the colonies by a size check first, because the three states differ in the length of the plasmid and length is the cheapest thing to measure. Grow each colony, prepare the plasmid DNA, cut it with a restriction enzyme whose site lies inside the insert, and run the products against a ladder: a single insert releases one fragment of the insert's length, two inserts release two such fragments, and re-closed vector with no insert releases none at all. The two inserts can also be in tandem in one plasmid or on two separate plasmids, and those are distinguished by a preparation that shows one band for a tandem arrangement and two bands for two molecules, which is why the crude lysate preparation rather than a purified plasmid is the more informative first step. A colony polymerase reaction that amplifies across the insert and the vector junction is the confirming test for any that the size screen leaves ambiguous, because a junction can only exist if the insert was actually joined into the vector rather than carried alongside it. The constants that matter are that every colony is treated identically, that the ladder is in the same gel as the samples, and that the control plasmid of known size is run alongside, since a size screen with no reference reports nothing.

questions.explanation: The three outcomes differ in two measurable ways, the total length of the plasmid and the number of insert copies inside it, so a screen that reads both resolves the ambiguity that a selectable marker alone cannot, because the marker reports the vector and not the insert.

questions.topic: Biotechnology: Testing a Blot Probe for Off-Target Binding

questions.stem: A blot of digested DNA gives three bands, but the laboratory expects only one fragment. Describe a test that would establish whether the extra bands come from the probe binding elsewhere rather than from extra copies of the target.

answer.exemplar: Run the same digested sample in two lanes of one gel and probe the two lanes with different strings. One lane uses the labelled probe as designed, and the other uses a probe of the same length and labelling taken from a different part of the molecule, chosen so that it cannot match the target. A band that appears in both lanes is therefore binding because of the probe's general properties, such as its tendency to stick to a repeated sequence or to the membrane, while a band that appears only in the target lane is a sequence the probe genuinely matches. Stringency is the second lever: re-probing the same membrane at a higher temperature and salt concentration removes weak matches, and any band that disappears was held on by partial complementarity rather than by a full match. The essential controls are the non-matching probe of matched labelling and stringency, and a lane containing a known positive sample, because a blot with no positive control cannot distinguish a clean result from a failed one. Holding the sample, the digestion and the wash conditions constant between lanes is what allows any difference in banding to be attributed to the probe rather than to the material.

questions.explanation: Non-specific binding and extra copies of the target both give extra bands in the designed-probe lane, so the discriminating control has to give the probe one difference only, namely what sequence it can match, which a non-matching probe of the same length and labelling achieves.

A twofold difference, so the sample held 4,000 copies because each cycle counts as one copy
options.misconception: counts a cycle as a single unit rather than as a doubling

options.text: An eightfold difference, so the sample held 8,000 copies because the standard reading is its own count

options.misconception: miscounts the cycle gap as four rather than the three actually given

questions.subject: BIOLOGY
questions.topic: Biotechnology: Why a Non-Pathogenic Strain Is Still Contained
questions.learningObjective: explain why containment is fitted even when the organism cannot cause disease
questions.stem: A laboratory works only with a strain that is not known to cause disease, and its safety statement claims the work carries no risk on that ground. Explain why containment is still fitted, and say what would have to be true for the claim to be reasonable.

answer.exemplar: Not causing disease is a statement about one property, virulence, and containment is fitted against several others that the same strain can have. A non-pathogenic organism can still be shed from the building in waste water, can still contaminate a person's clothing and travel to another laboratory, and can still be adapted by acquiring a mobile element that makes it pathogenic, which is a recognised route by which innocuous laboratory strains become causes of infection in people. A strain can also be misidentified, and the identification is what every containment decision rests on, so the fitment is a response to the possibility of error as much as to the biology. Containment is therefore not a judgement that the organism is dangerous; it is a set of barriers that limit what happens if that judgement is wrong, which is why the barriers are chosen for the harm that would follow a release rather than for the harm the organism is known to cause. For the claim to be reasonable the strain would have to be shown not to cause disease in the host most likely to receive it, its identity confirmed independently of the culture label, and the work done in a way that contains whatever else might be present, since a laboratory rarely has only one organism in it. The honest formulation is that the risk is low and bounded, not that it is absent, because a risk described as absent stops being examined while a risk described as bounded is examined every time.

questions.explanation: The explanation has to separate the property the claim relies on, which is virulence, from the several properties containment guards against, and then to say that containment is a response to being wrong about the first, which is what the second is for.
questions.hint: Ask how many different properties of an organism containment is guarding against, and how many of them being absent the claim names.

questions.learningObjective: order the steps that build a recombinant plasmid and recover transformed cells
questions.stem: Put these five steps in the order they are carried out to build a recombinant plasmid and recover cells that carry it.

Join the fragment into the opened vector with a ligase so that one recombinant molecule forms

Grow the cells on a medium on which only those carrying the plasmid's marker survive
Screen the colonies that grow, to confirm that the plasmid carries the intended insert

Delivery has to precede selection, because selection is a property of cells rather than of molecules and there is nothing to select in a tube. Selection has to precede screening, because screening a colony by any method requires a colony, and colonies that did not take up the plasmid would only waste the effort. The tempting wrong order that screens before selecting fails because there is no colony yet, and the order that selects before joining fails because no cell has a plasmid to carry the marker.

Because it cuts the message into pieces before copying, so that each piece can be extended separately
options.misconception: believes the enzyme fragments the template as a necessary part of copying it

options.text: Because it removes the added tail from the message before reading it, so the code is exposed
options.misconception: believes the added tail must be stripped off before the message can be read

options.text: Because it adds the message's own nucleotides back in, rebuilding a double-stranded copy from the single strand
options.misconception: believes the enzyme repairs the template instead of copying from it

questions.topic: Biotechnology: What a Knock-Out and a Knock-In Each Achieve

A knock-out removes the gene in one cell type, while a knock-in removes it in every cell type
options.misconception: believes the distinction is which tissue is affected rather than what is changed

options.text: A knock-out removes the gene before birth, while a knock-in removes it after the organism is grown
options.misconception: believes the distinction is when the change is made rather than what it does

options.text: A knock-out removes the gene's product, while a knock-in removes the gene that makes it
options.misconception: believes knock-in acts on a protein rather than on the DNA

A knock-in places a chosen sequence at the locus, which is how a tagged version, a modified version or a replacement is installed in its normal position rather than somewhere else. The vessel is weighed and the gas leaving it is measured. When the glucose is exhausted, the liquid is found to contain 511 grams of ethanol and the gas collected over the run totals 489 grams of carbon dioxide. The balance of the fermenter is unchanged apart from the material in and out.

The two products exceed the input, because 511 plus 489 is more than the glucose that was charged
options.misconception: mis-adds the two figures and concludes that material was created

options.misconception: believes material that left the fermenter cannot have come from the charge

options.text: Most of the glucose became something unmeasured, because 1,000 minus 511 is larger than the gas figure
options.misconception: subtracts only one product and treats the balance as a missing mass

The belief that the gas did not come from the charge fails because the only carbon in the system was in the glucose. The belief that a missing mass remains fails because the only subtraction that makes sense is both products against the charge.

A colony is grown, its plasmid is prepared, and the plasmid is cut with two enzymes together: the first cuts the vector once at a site 500 base pairs from one end of the inserted fragment, and the second cuts the vector at its own single site. A separate preparation from the same colony is cut with the first enzyme alone. A ladder of known lengths is run in the same gel.

The double digest gives 5,400 and 1,600, and the single digest gives one band at 7,000

options.text: The double digest gives 6,900 and 100, and the single digest gives two bands at 1,600 and 5,400

options.text: The double digest gives 1,600 and 5,400, and the single digest gives nothing because the insert blocks both sites

questions.subject: BIOLOGY
questions.topic: Biotechnology: Judging Amplification Efficiency From a Ten-Cycle Drop
questions.learningObjective: assess how close a ten-cycle fall comes to perfect doubling

stimulus.body: Laboratory note (written for this course): A reaction begins with 1,000,000 copies of the target and the threshold is reached at 1,000 copies after ten complete cycles, with a reaction in which a cycle ought to double the count exactly. Perfect doubling over ten cycles would take 1,000,000 down to 1,000,000 divided by 2 to the tenth, which is 977. A drop to 1,000 rather than 977 means the reaction is not doubling quite as fast as it should.

questions.stem: Using only the laboratory note, how close is this reaction to perfect doubling?

options.text: Very close, since a 1.995-fold gain each cycle is about 99.5 per cent of perfect doubling
Very poor, since reaching 1,000 from a million in ten cycles is a thousandfold fall and cannot be efficient
options.misconception: reads a three-orders-of-magnitude fall as evidence that amplification failed

options.text: Exactly perfect, since 1,000 and 977 are close enough to be the same number on a gel
options.misconception: treats two nearby figures as identical when the ratio is what is being measured

options.text: Unknown, since a gain per cycle cannot be worked out from two endpoint figures alone
options.misconception: believes the per-cycle factor is not recoverable from a stated starting and ending count

questions.explanation: The per-cycle gain is the starting count divided by the ending count, then the tenth root of that, which works out at about 1.995 against a perfect 2, so the reaction is achieving roughly 99.5 per cent of full doubling. The gap between 977 and 1,000 looks large in absolute terms and is tiny in the terms that matter, because the amplification is a chain of ten multiplications and a factor of 1.007 per cycle compounds into the observed 2.3 per cent. That compounding is the reason efficiency is quoted as a percentage per cycle rather than as an end-point difference, and it is also why a reaction at 90 per cent efficiency loses a full doubling every ten cycles. The tempting belief that a thousandfold fall is poor fails because ten perfect doublings is exactly a thousandfold fall, so the figure confirms rather than contradicts efficiency. The belief that 1,000 and 977 are identical fails because the ratio, not the difference, is the measurement. The belief that the factor is unrecoverable fails because two endpoints over a known number of cycles determine it completely.
questions.hint: Take the thousandfold fall over ten cycles, then find the tenth root of it.

questions.topic: Biotechnology: Testing a Claim That Sterility Was Achieved
questions.learningObjective: design a control that could falsify a claim of sterility
questions.stem: A laboratory claims a treated medium is sterile. Describe a test that would show the claim is false, and name the control that makes a negative result meaningful.

answer.exemplar: Inoculate the treated medium into an equally suitable medium that favours growth, including the step that favours spore germination, and look for growth over a period long enough for a spore to germinate and become visible. To make the result interpretable, run the identical inoculations from a batch of the same medium that was deliberately left untreated, which is the control that shows the test is capable of detecting an organism that is present, and a further control of sterile medium with no inoculum added, which shows whether anything is growing that the medium brought with it. The two controls answer different failures: an untreated positive control that stays clear means the test cannot detect contamination rather than that there is none, and a no-inoculum control that grows means the medium or the handling introduced something and the negative result is worthless. Two practical details matter as much as the design. The incubation must be long enough and the conditions must favour spore germination, because the usual cause of a false claim of sterility is a test that was incubated too briefly to let a surviving spore show itself. And the volume sampled has to be sufficient, since sterilisation is a probability rather than a guarantee and a small sample can miss the rare survivor, which is why the test checks a stated fraction of the batch.
answer.explanation: The design has to include a positive control and a negative control because a negative result is uninformative without them: without the positive one you cannot tell a clean batch from a test that does not work, and without the negative one you cannot rule out contamination carried in by the medium or the handling.

questions.topic: Biotechnology: Working Out an Unknown From a Two-Point Calibration
questions.learningObjective: convert a sample reading into a concentration using a calibration line
questions.stem: A bioassay is calibrated at two known concentrations: a blank at zero units per millilitre reads 0.4 units of signal, and a standard at 20 units per millilitre reads 12.4 units of signal. A sample of unknown concentration reads 7.6. First work out the calibration, then the sample's concentration.

options.text: A rise of 0.6 per unit per millilitre from a 0.4 baseline, and the sample holds 12 units per millilitre
A rise of 12.0 per unit per millilitre from a 0.4 baseline, and the sample holds 0.6 units per millilitre
options.misconception: reports the total signal rise as though it were the slope per unit

options.text: A rise of 0.6 per unit per millilitre from a 0.4 baseline, and the sample holds 5.2 units per millilitre
options.misconception: subtracts the blank from the sample without dividing by the slope

options.text: A rise of 0.3 per unit per millilitre from a 0.4 baseline, and the sample holds 24 units per millilitre
options.misconception: halves the concentration range, treating the two standards as the half- and full-scale

questions.explanation: The calibration line has a slope equal to the change in signal over the change in concentration, which is 12.4 minus 0.4 over 20 minus 0, giving 12 over 20 and so 0.6 units of signal per unit per millilitre, and it has an intercept of 0.4, which is the blank reading and is subtracted before the slope is applied. The sample's signal above its blank is 7.6 minus 0.4, which is 7.2, and 7.2 divided by 0.6 is 12 units per millilitre. Back-substitution confirms it: 0.4 plus 0.6 times 12 is 7.6, the reading that was given. Two features of a real assay are hidden in the numbers. The intercept is not zero because a blank contains everything except the target, and treating the raw reading as the signal overstates every result. And a two-point calibration is only worth having if the response really is linear across the range, which is why a real assay runs several standards and looks for a straight line before trusting an extrapolation to the top of the range. The tempting belief that the total signal rise is the slope fails because the slope is per unit of concentration. The belief that 5.2 is the concentration forgets to divide by the slope. The belief that 20 units is the full scale fails because nothing in the note says the range stops there.
questions.hint: Find the signal change per unit of concentration, subtract the blank from the sample, then divide.

questions.subject: BIOLOGY
questions.topic: Biotechnology: Why a Safety Claim Outruns Its Barriers
questions.learningObjective: explain how a containment mechanism can contradict a claim of no effect
questions.stem: A biotechnology is described as having no effect on the organisms that share the laboratory with it, and containment is fitted anyway. Explain how the containment contradicts that claim, and say what the claim would need in order to hold.

answer.exemplar: A containment mechanism is a set of barriers, and a barrier only exists where something is being held back, so the presence of fitted containment is itself a statement that an effect was considered possible. The contradiction is sharper than that, though, because a barrier fitted to a real channel of escape is a channel that was judged worth closing: a cabinet draws air in and passes it through a filter rather than simply sealing the room, which means the design assumes air leaves the work and has to be treated, and a sealed vessel is chosen over an open one for the same reason. A filter of a stated pore size is the sharpest case, because a barrier that is specified by what it can and cannot stop is a claim that the unfiltered route would let something through, and if nothing could get out there would be no reason to specify a pore size at all. For the original claim to hold it would have to be a claim about the whole pathway rather than about the organism in isolation: no route of escape, no route of transfer, no plausible route by which the material acquires the properties that make it harmful, and independent confirmation that the material in use is the one characterised. That standard is rarely reachable, which is why the defensible formulation is that the risk is small and bounded, not that it is absent. A claim of absence stops being examined the moment it is made, whereas a claim of bounded risk comes with a level that can be checked and a barrier that can be tested, and that is the difference the containment mechanism is actually documenting.

questions.explanation: The explanation has to make the contradiction structural rather than a matter of caution, because a barrier is evidence of a judged possible effect, and then it has to say what a defensible claim would have to cover, which is the whole route out rather than the organism alone.
questions.hint: Ask what the presence of a barrier implies about whether something was expected to pass through it.

questions.topic: Biotechnology: Ordering the Chain From a Sample to a Reading
questions.learningObjective: order the stages that turn a sample into a calibrated numerical result
questions.stem: Put these five stages in the order a measurement passes through them in a calibrated assay.

options.text: A defined sample is introduced onto the sensing surface in a known amount
The target in the sample binds the recognition element chosen to match it
The binding event is converted into a change in the device's electrical or optical output
The output is measured and compared against a calibration built from known amounts
The result is reported with the range over which the calibration can be trusted

questions.explanation: The chain is a sequence of dependencies, and each stage is meaningless without the one before it. The sample has to arrive in a known amount because the output is otherwise a property of how much was delivered rather than of what was in it. The binding has to happen before any output, because binding is the only event carrying information about the target. The transduction has to happen before the measurement, because a binding event produces no reading and the device exists to convert one into the other. The comparison against a calibration has to happen after the measurement, because a calibration relates an output to a known input and neither exists until both are present. Reporting with the trusted range comes last because a number without its range is not an answer, since a calibration is only straight over the range in which the standards were run and a result beyond them is an extrapolation. The wrong order that measures before the binding fails because there is nothing to measure. The wrong order that compares before the output is converted fails because the signal does not exist yet.

questions.subject: BIOLOGY
questions.topic: Bioinformatics: What a Database Hit Does and Does Not Mean
questions.learningObjective: interpret what a similarity search reports and what it does not establish
questions.stem: A sequence is submitted to a similarity search and five matches are returned, one with an expected value of 1 in 10^40. What does that result establish?

options.text: That a similar sequence exists and is unlikely to have matched by chance, not that it has the same function
That the matching sequence performs the same role in its own organism, because similarity implies function
options.misconception: believes sequence similarity alone establishes what a gene does

options.text: That the two sequences are identical throughout, because such a low expected value leaves no room for difference
options.misconception: believes a strong statistical score means the sequences are the same

options.text: That the query sequence has no closer relative, since anything closer would have been listed first
options.misconception: believes the order of returned hits reports the query's true relatedness

questions.explanation: An expected value is a statement about chance: a value of 1 in 10^40 means the match is not expected to arise from random sequence comparison, which is a claim about how improbable the alignment is and nothing more. It says a similar sequence is present in the database; it does not say what that sequence does, because many different functions are built from related folds and a substantial fraction of genes have no known function at all, so a hit is a lead to be tested rather than a conclusion. It also does not mean the sequences are identical, since the expected value is a function of the alignment's length as well as its score, and a long weak alignment can reach a very small value. Two further limits are worth stating: the result depends on the database, since a hit in a large database is harder to obtain by chance and a small expected value is only meaningful relative to that database's size, and the order of the returned hits is a ranking by score rather than a report of the query's actual relatives. The tempting belief that similarity implies function fails because that is a hypothesis and an often incorrect one. The belief that a low score means identity fails because the score and the identity are different quantities. The belief that the list is ordered by relatedness fails because the list is ordered by score.
questions.hint: Ask what an expected value is calculated from, and what it is a statement about.

questions.subject: BIOLOGY
questions.topic: Bioinformatics: Reading Relatedness Off an Aligned Set of Sequences
questions.learningObjective: infer which sequences group together from a set of aligned positions
questions.stem: Four sequences are aligned over eight positions, and a tree is drawn so that each branch length shows how much change separates the groups. What does the grouping rest on?

options.text: Which pair of sequences shares the most positions and the fewest differences between them
Which sequences have the most functional constraints, since a constrained sequence changes less often
options.misconception: believes conservation reports function rather than relatedness

options.text: Which sequences were sampled from the most different habitats, since habitat drives divergence
options.misconception: believes the grouping is read from where the organisms were sampled

options.text: Which sequences were sequenced most recently, since newer data is assumed to be closer
options.misconception: believes the date of a sequence determines its placement

questions.explanation: The grouping rests on shared differences: two sequences are placed together when they carry the same changes relative to the others, because shared derived states are the evidence of common descent, and the number of differences between them sets the branch length. Two sequences that differ at one position and agree everywhere else are closer than two that differ at five, and the whole tree is chosen to need the fewest total changes, which is why it is built by a rule rather than drawn by eye. The logic is the same as the argument from shared derived characters in classical systematics, applied to positions in a sequence instead of to form. The limiting assumption is worth naming, because it is what the method rests on: changes are assumed to be rare and to occur by chance, so that a shared position is more likely to have been inherited than to have arisen twice. The tempting belief that conservation reports function fails because a sequence can be highly conserved and still have no known function, and because a group can be very similar and have no function in common. The belief that habitat drives the grouping fails because the habitat is not in the alignment. The belief that sequencing date matters fails because the date is a property of the record and not of the molecule.
questions.hint: Ask which numbers from the alignment actually enter the calculation of a branch length.

questions.topic: Bioinformatics: Where a Predicted Structure Cannot Be Trusted
questions.learningObjective: state the cases in which a predicted structure is weakest
questions.stem: Structure prediction is now good enough to be useful for many single-chain proteins. In which of these cases is it least dependable?

For a single chain of ordinary length whose fold is stable on its own in a familiar environment
options.misconception: believes the well-ordered single-chain case is the unreliable one

options.misconception: believes a protein with a known structure is harder to predict than an unknown one

options.misconception: believes internal repetition makes a prediction less reliable

questions.topic: Biosafety: Matching an Agent to a Containment Level
questions.learningObjective: assign a working practice to a stated level of biological hazard
questions.stem: Work is to be carried out on an agent that can kill people by the respiratory route and for which no reliable vaccine or treatment exists. Which containment is called for?

options.misconception: believes a small working volume removes the hazard entirely

options.text: A middle level with gloves and a cabinet, since the absence of a treatment is not a containment factor
options.misconception: believes the availability of a treatment does not set the level

questions.explanation: The level is set by three properties of the agent, which are the route of harm, whether the harm is serious or lethal, and whether a vaccine or treatment exists to limit the consequences if someone is exposed. An agent that can kill by the respiratory route, that is lethal, and that has no vaccine or treatment scores at the top of all three and belongs in the highest containment, where the work is done in a cabinet that draws air in and passes it through a filter, entry is controlled and monitored, and the plumbing and the effluent are treated separately. The reason the highest level is needed is not caution in general but the combination: a respiratory route means an aerosol is the likely accident, and no treatment means an accident cannot be undone. The lower levels exist for agents that score lower on those same three properties, and a non-pathogenic organism is worked with only ordinary good practice because there is nothing to protect against. The tempting belief that a small volume removes the hazard fails because an aerosol does not care how much was present. The belief that the absence of a treatment is not a factor has it exactly backwards, since that is one of the three things the level is set by. options.misconception: believes the liquid and surface distinction decides the sterilisation question

Filtration is a good method for a solution and a poor one for spores, and radiation and long contact with a chemical can each destroy spores given enough. The belief that cost decides it fails because the criterion is what is destroyed, not what is paid. options.text: One can be inherited by people who were never consented, while the other concerns only the person treated
One is easier to perform, so it should be preferred wherever the technical problem is simpler
options.misconception: believes ease of performance is what turns on the ethical distinction

options.text: One affects a single person and the other affects a whole population's environment instead
options.misconception: confuses the two cases with the difference between individual and collective effects

options.text: One can be undone by a later treatment, while the other is permanent in every cell from the start
options.misconception: reverses the cases, since only a body-cell change is confined to one person

questions.explanation: The ethical difference is about consent and about who bears the consequences. A body-cell change is confined to the person treated, who can be asked whether they want it, and the change is in every cell descended from the one that received it but in no gamete, so nobody else is affected by default. A germline change is in the gametes, so it can reach people who are not yet born, who cannot be asked, and it cannot be withdrawn from them afterwards, so a mistake made with good intentions is permanent for every descendant. That asymmetry is what the debate is about, and it is why the position taken on the second is different in kind from the first, and why the framing of the choice matters as much as the science: a therapy offered to one patient is a different kind of act from an alteration whose effects are spread across an unbounded number of unconsenting people. The uncertainties compound it, since a germline change's later effects are not fully predictable from its immediate ones, and the affected party is precisely the party unable to object. The tempting belief that ease of performance is the point fails because technical difficulty is an engineering matter, not an ethical one. The belief that this is a population-versus-environment case fails because both are individual medical acts. The belief that the body-cell case is the permanent one fails because confinement to one person is what makes it reversible in principle.

questions.topic: Biotechnology: Following a Construct Through Two Generations
questions.learningObjective: compute how a construct's carrier count changes between generations

stimulus.body: Field record (written for this course): A closed population of 200 individuals is given a release of 20 individuals homozygous for a construct whose action in the germ line copies it into the matching chromosome, so that every gamete from a carrier carries it. All other individuals are homozygous for the ordinary version. Gametes combine at random and the population is replaced each generation with 200 new individuals. Under ordinary inheritance a carrier passes the construct to half its gametes.

questions.stem: Using only the field record, how many of the 200 offspring are expected to carry the construct?

options.text: About 38 in the first generation, and about 69 in the second with the construct but 36 without
About 38 in the first generation, and about 38 again in the second either way, since the release is fixed
options.misconception: believes a fixed release of homozygotes produces a fixed count in every generation

options.text: About 200 in the first generation, because the construct is copied into every gamete it meets
options.misconception: confuses copying within a carrier with spreading through the whole population

options.text: About 20 in the first generation, and about 10 in the second as carriers dilute the construct
options.misconception: assumes dilution alone determines the count and ignores random mating

questions.explanation: The first generation is the same either way and that is the instructive part: 20 homozygous individuals each contribute two gametes carrying the construct, so 40 of the 400 gametes carry it, a frequency of 0.1, and an offspring receives two gametes, so the chance of at least one is 1 minus 0.9 squared, which is 0.19, and 200 times that is 38. Ordinary inheritance and the construct behave identically here because a homozygote passes its allele to all of its gametes under both. The difference appears in the second generation, because the 38 carriers are now heterozygous and the two mechanisms part company: with the construct every gamete they make carries it, giving 76 of 400 and 1 minus 0.81 squared, which is about 69 carriers, while under ordinary inheritance only half their gametes do, giving 38 of 400 and about 36 carriers. The construct therefore does not spread by being released many times but by being inherited more often than a copy would be, and the gap widens in later generations. The tempting belief that the count is fixed fails because the 38 carriers determine the next generation's gametes. The belief that all 200 become carriers fails because copying happens inside a carrier, not between unrelated individuals. The belief that dilution alone sets the count fails because random mating of a minority does not make the next generation the same size as the release.
questions.hint: Work out the fraction of gametes carrying the construct in each generation, then use two gametes per offspring.

questions.topic: Immunology: Reading a Response to a Single-Dose Vaccine
questions.learningObjective: infer what a recorded antibody response shows about the vaccine's action

stimulus.body: Laboratory note (written for this course): Twenty people are given one dose of a vaccine built from a single purified protein from an organism, and twenty are given an inert injection. Blood is taken before the dose, four weeks after it, and a year after it. In the vaccinated group the antibody level against that protein rises well above its starting value by four weeks and is still above it a year later, with no detectable rise in the antibody level against an unrelated protein. In the untreated group nothing changes. When the same people are later exposed to the whole organism, the antibody level against the protein rises much further and much faster than it did after the dose alone.

questions.stem: Using only the laboratory note, which single reading best fits what happened?

options.text: The dose raised antibody to that protein specifically, and left a population able to respond faster later
The dose raised antibody generally, and the later rise shows the organism was present in the dose
options.misconception: believes the response was general and that the whole organism was present in the dose

options.text: The dose established a population of the organism, which the later exposure then confirmed
options.misconception: believes a purified protein can establish a population that multiplies in the body

options.text: The dose did nothing, and the later rise is the first response the group ever made
options.misconception: reads the small control response as a failure of the dose rather than as a response

Antibody against the chosen protein rose and antibody against an unrelated protein did not, so the response was directed at the target rather than being a general activation of the immune system, which is the expected behaviour of a vaccine presenting a single defined target. The untreated group changing nothing shows the rise was not a property of the measurement or of the passage of a year. The larger and faster response on later exposure to the whole organism is the signature of a memory population having formed: when the organism arrives, the memory cells respond in days rather than the weeks a first response takes, and the amount produced is far greater, which is the whole purpose of the dose. The tempting belief that the response was general fails because the control protein showed no rise. The belief that the organism was in the dose fails because a purified protein is not a population of anything and cannot multiply. The belief that the dose did nothing fails because a measurable rise followed it and the later response was faster, which is the opposite of no effect.
questions.hint: Ask what the unrelated-protein control rules out, and what a faster second response means.

questions.subject: BIOLOGY
questions.topic: Biotechnology: Reading an Enzyme Process at Its Working Temperature
questions.learningObjective: interpret process data using the enzyme's own temperature requirement

stimulus.body: Laboratory note (written for this course): Two vats of starch slurry are run side by side. In the first, the slurry is held at 30 degrees Celsius and an enzyme is added; the viscosity stays high and the starch is not broken down. In the second, the slurry is raised to 85 degrees, which liquefies it so that the viscosity falls sharply, and the same enzyme is then added; the viscosity falls further and the fluid tests as a simple sugar rather than as starch. Measuring the fluid in the second vat gives about 900 grams of sugar for every 1,000 grams of starch charged.

questions.stem: Using only the laboratory note, which single reading explains both results?

options.text: The enzyme works only at the higher temperature, where heating and the reaction proceed as one step
The enzyme works at both temperatures, so the first vat failed only because it was stirred too slowly
options.misconception: attributes the unchanged first vat to stirring rather than to the temperature the enzyme needs

options.text: The enzyme is destroyed at the higher temperature, so the second result came from heating alone
options.misconception: claims heat destroyed the enzyme, ignoring that the product rose after it was added

options.text: The enzyme needs a companion enzyme that was present in one vat and not the other
options.misconception: invents a second enzyme present in one vat and absent from the other with no evidence

questions.explanation: The two results are explained by one property, which is the temperature the enzyme actually works at. At 30 degrees the starch is a thick, tangled structure and the enzyme does not act on it, so nothing changes; at 85 degrees the same slurry has been broken open by heating into something the enzyme can work on, and the enzyme then converts it to a simple sugar, which is why the second vat tests as sugar and the first does not. The masses are consistent with that, since a thousand grams of starch yields about nine hundred grams of sugar and the remaining hundred grams of mass leaves as water that is consumed in joining the sugar units together, so nothing is created and the figure is a check rather than a coincidence. The practical lesson is the one an industrial process exists to exploit: choosing an enzyme whose working temperature matches the temperature the material has to be heated to anyway collapses two steps into one and saves the energy of a separate cooling and reheating. The tempting belief that the enzyme works at both temperatures fails because the first vat shows it does nothing at 30. The belief that it is destroyed at 85 fails because it clearly acted there. The belief that a companion enzyme is needed fails because the record shows the same enzyme and a different temperature.
questions.hint: Ask what the temperature did to the starch before the enzyme arrived, and what the enzyme then did to it.

questions.subject: BIOLOGY
questions.topic: Bioinformatics: Choosing the Grouping That Needs Fewest Changes
questions.learningObjective: apply parsimony to a character matrix to pick a grouping

stimulus.body: Laboratory note (written for this course): Four sequences are aligned across eight positions. At positions 1, 2, 3 and 4 sequences C and D both carry a residue that A and B do not. At position 5 all four carry the same residue. At position 6 only B differs, at position 7 only C differs, and at position 8 only D differs. A, B, C and D differ from one another at 1, 2, 2 and 5 positions respectively in the pairs A with B, A with C, C with D, and A with D. Three candidate groupings are compared by counting the fewest changes each would need.

questions.stem: Using only the laboratory note, which grouping is best supported, and why?

options.text: C with D beside each other, because grouping them together accounts for the four shared residues in one change
A with C beside each other, because the pair is closest since A and C differ at only one position
options.misconception: quotes a one-position difference that the record does not give and ignores the four shared positions

options.text: B with C beside each other, because a lone difference in one sequence is best placed on its own branch
options.misconception: lets a unique difference on one sequence drive the grouping, though it costs the same either way

options.text: B with D beside each other, because a grouping that separates the shared residues needs the most changes
options.misconception: reverses the parsimony rule, treating the grouping needing most changes as the best

questions.explanation: The four positions where C and D share a residue that A and B lack are what decide it, because a shared difference is evidence of a common ancestor, and a grouping that puts C and D together explains all four in a single change while any grouping that separates them needs each shared position changed twice. Counting the minimum for each candidate gives seven changes for the grouping that keeps C and D together against eleven for either of the two that split them, and the four extra changes are exactly the cost of separating a pair that shares four derived states. The three positions where one sequence differs on its own do not decide anything, because a unique difference costs one change on whatever grouping is chosen. The rule being applied is parsimony, and the assumption under it is that changes are rare and independent, so the simplest history is the most likely one. The tempting belief that A and C are closest fails because the note itself gives five differences for that pair against one for A and B, so the pair with fewest differences is A with B, not A with C. The belief that a lone difference should drive the grouping fails because it costs the same on every grouping. The belief that separating the shared residues is preferable fails because it is exactly what raises the change count from seven to eleven.
questions.hint: Ask which candidate grouping explains the four shared residues with the fewest separate changes.
